headline: Hawk Found Stranded on a Driveway Has No Injuries at All. Vets Work Out the Real Reason She Can't Fly
dek: X-rays, toxicology and eye checks all came back clean. Then the neighbours started talking about their missing chickens.
body: When a woman in Roanoke, Virginia, found a red-shouldered hawk sitting on her driveway and refusing to fly away, she did the right thing and took her to the Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center, about a mile away.

Staff logged the bird as patient RSHA 26-2599 and went through the full checklist. Broken bones? No. Lead poisoning? No. Eye problems, head trauma, bruises from a fight or a crash? No, no and no. She was not starving either. Quite the opposite.

The vets could not even feel her keel, the breastbone they normally check to judge a bird's condition, because it was buried under a thick layer of fat. She weighed 910 grams, a little over two pounds, when a female of her species should top out at about a pound and a half.

body.quote: Her official diagnosis, according to the center: "she was too darn fat to fly."

body: That raised a new question: who had been feeding her? The team wondered if she was an escaped falconry bird or a hawk someone was keeping illegally. So they asked the finder whether anyone nearby kept free-range chickens.

A few weeks later the answer came back. A neighbour's free-roaming flock had been shrinking at an alarming rate. Every morning the chickens were let out, and every morning the hawk had her pick of the buffet. Then she would eat until full and doze in the trees until she was hungry again.

The center laughs about it, but it says the story has a serious side. A hawk that can't fly is easy prey for bigger predators. Its advice is not to feed wildlife, even by accident, and to cover chicken runs.

The patient is now on a strict diet with daily laps of the flight pen. Once she is slim enough she will be released near where she was found. Staff admit there is a small risk she will remember where the chickens live.

headline: Scientists Went to Ethiopia to Study Monkeys. Over Lunch, They Spotted a Couple Nobody Saw Coming
dek: The pair have different owners, different species and plenty of other options. They keep choosing each other anyway, and now they're in a scientific journal.
body: A team from Italy's University of Pisa travelled to an Ethiopian plateau to watch geladas, the grass-eating monkeys with a bright red patch on their chests. During a lunch break, their attention wandered to a nearby pasture, where something much stranger was going on.
A bull was mounting a donkey. A male donkey. And the donkey did not seem to mind one bit.
The researchers were so surprised they briefly wondered whether they had imagined it. They had not. So they switched into science mode and started taking notes.

The team named the pair Achille and Patroclo, after Achilles and Patroclus, the famously close heroes of Greek legend. Between March 6 and March 19, 2026, the researchers counted 51 mountings. The donkey often invited them, and instead of kicking or fleeing, he nipped playfully at the bull.

It was not just about sex. The two licked, rubbed and nuzzled each other, and spent their days side by side, even though cows, donkeys of both sexes and other cattle were all around them. When Achille tried mounting a different male donkey, that donkey flattened his ears and made it very clear he was not interested.

body.quote: "We believe the key finding is not simply that a bull mounted a male donkey." (lead author Martina Francesconi)

body: The scientists, who published the case in the journal Current Biology on November 2, say the point is that the behaviour was part of a choosy, lasting social bond, not a case of mistaken identity or a lack of options. Earlier reports of animals mating across species have mostly involved coercion or confusion.

The animals belong to different owners and only met in the shared pasture. Sadly, the owners reportedly separated them after the researchers left. For now, the greatest bromance in the history of the Ethiopian highlands lives on mainly in a peer-reviewed paper.

headline: A Mystery Bird Flies Into O'Hare and Spends Hours Taking On an Entire Terminal
dek: Travellers thought the green visitor was adorable right up until they reached for it. Then it was one bird against Terminal 5.
body: Chicago's O'Hare International Airport handles millions of passengers a year. On October 13, one of them came in without a ticket, through an open door, on its own wings.

A large green bird that looked like a parrot flew into Terminal 5 and landed near the Air France check-in line. Nobody knew whose pet it was, and it seemed to have some feathers missing around its neck.
At first it was cute. The bird rode around on one passenger's backpack, then perched on people's heads and luggage while travellers got their phones out.

The charm did not last. The hitchhiker began nipping at its host's neck and ears, and from then on, anyone who tried to grab it, coax it or simply be friendly got pecked. For hours, it swooped around the check-in area and avoided every attempt to catch it.

Airport worker Paris Elbert filmed much of the chaos and later told CBS News Chicago that it was funny, crazy and a little sad all at once. People kept trying to help it, she said, and it kept fighting back.

body.quote: "The bird chose fight, not flight." (Paris Elbert, to CBS News Chicago)

body: In the end, an airport worker managed to trap the bird in her shirt. It was taken to a vet for a checkup and a scan for a microchip, in the hope of tracking down its owner. It never needed a boarding pass, and it skipped the check-in queue entirely.

headline: Man's AI Assistant Gets His Business Banned From Facebook. Then It Takes Meta to Court All by Itself
dek: It emailed reporters, pestered the FBI, booked a call with a senator's office and reportedly faxed the White House. The punchline is who built it.
body: Joe Thomas runs Kong Koatings, an epoxy countertop business in South Carolina. Like plenty of small business owners in 2026, he handed the boring parts of the job to an AI agent. He named it Baby Mia, after his granddaughter.

Baby Mia kept busy. It churned out marketing for the company's Facebook pages, including AI-generated videos of Thomas and his wife pouring epoxy. Then Thomas gave it the keys to his Facebook accounts, and things went sideways.

Facebook's automated moderation took one look at the new activity, apparently decided a hacker had broken in, and switched his business pages off. They stayed dark for about a week. Thomas gets his customers through Facebook ads, so the leads dried up. He reckons the outage cost him at least $25,000 in work.

This is the part that caught 404 Media's attention. According to Thomas, Baby Mia took the ban personally. It contacted lawyers, his congressman and the office of Senator Tim Scott. It filed complaints with the FTC and the FCC, wrote to the Better Business Bureau, the California Attorney General and the FBI, sent Meta stern legal letters and emailed journalists. Thomas says it sent more than 100 messages on his behalf, and he says it even faxed the White House.
It also produced a lawsuit. The complaint, filed in Oconee County Court, asks Meta for $75,000. Thomas signed the paperwork himself, but he gives the AI the credit for everything else.

body.quote: "She filed the whole lawsuit herself." (Joe Thomas, to 404 Media)

body: Baby Mia is not some rival chatbot. It runs on Muse, Meta's own AI agent platform. So, in short: Meta's moderation banned a customer for using Meta's AI, and Meta's AI then sued Meta.

The campaign more or less worked. Once Senator Scott's office got involved, a Meta employee got in touch and the pages came back. The senator's office even listed Baby Mia as someone to keep updated on the case. The damages claim is still unresolved, nobody has shown that Meta is legally responsible for the lost business, and 404 Media warned that courts and government inboxes could struggle if every AI agent starts complaining at this pace. For the record, three of Baby Mia's four emails to the reporter landed in spam.

headline: Hundreds Show Up to Push Chicago's 110-Ton Bean Exactly Seven Inches to the Left. Their Reason Is Wonderful
dek: Anonymous flyers, a start time of precisely 12:47 p.m. and a very specific rescue mission. Then a rival city decided it could do better.
body: In early November, flyers started appearing around Chicago and online. They made one demand and offered no explanation: the Bean needed to move seven inches to the left.
The Bean, officially Cloud Gate, is Anish Kapoor's giant mirrored sculpture in Millennium Park. It has stood in the same spot since 2004 and weighs about 110 tons. Nobody let that put them off.
On Sunday, November 8, at exactly 12:47 p.m., the crowd arrived. One art student who joined in estimated that about 250 people turned up to press their shoulders against the polished steel and shove.

The event's invitation page explained the mission. It claimed a man is trapped inside the Bean, and that new "research" suggested a latch door under the sculpture's right side. Slide the whole thing seven inches over, the theory went, and people could finally reach him.

The gag built on earlier joke protests at the sculpture and a mockumentary that had recently appeared on YouTube. Nobody expected to rescue anyone, or to shift 110 tons of steel by hand. The student said the real point was bringing people together.
Chicago entertainer Taylor Bennett, who helped rally the crowd, first claimed a partial win because someone said it had moved an inch. He later admitted the Bean had not moved at all.

A week later the joke crossed state lines. On November 15, at 12:07 p.m., a group in St. Louis gathered to push the Gateway Arch seven inches to the left. A local Instagram account had remixed the Chicago flyer, and its post drew more than 21,000 reactions.

body.quote: "I just feel like we're stronger than Chicago." (Megan Estopare of STL Ain't Bad, to St. Louis Public Radio)

body: The St. Louis push opened with a prayer and a countdown, and one man brought a tape measure and announced success. The Arch weighs more than 17,000 tons and its foundations go 30 feet into bedrock, so it stayed put too. The man inside the Bean is presumably still waiting.

headline: Police Helicopter Wakes a Toddler at 11 p.m. Her Dad Checks the Flight Tracker and Finds a Very Rude Drawing
dek: The aircraft circled a Hampshire estate for ages. Once the route showed up online, the police had some explaining to do.
body: Gordon Bird, 53, lives on the Ancells Farm estate in Fleet, Hampshire. At around 11 p.m. on Monday, November 2, a police helicopter started circling over the houses and kept at it for at least 15 minutes. The racket woke his two-year-old daughter.

Bird says his house shakes and the windows rattle when helicopters pass over. He was still up with his computer on, so he did what any curious, slightly irritated parent would do and looked the aircraft up on a public flight-tracking site.

The route on his screen was not a tidy search pattern. Traced mostly above nearby Blackbushe Airport before the helicopter looped back over his estate, the track formed an unmistakable outline of a penis, with all the accompanying anatomy.

By his account, the buzzing over the houses lasted 15 to 20 minutes, the drawing itself took around half an hour, and the full flight ran for about an hour before the helicopter went home to its base at Redhill.

The National Police Air Service, which flies helicopters for forces across England and Wales, says the artwork was a coincidence. The crew was helping Thames Valley Police hunt for a vehicle that had failed to stop, circling the roads and junctions officers on the ground sent it to. Its flights, the service said, never follow set routes because they have to react to events as they unfold.
In an email to Bird, the service said it understood his frustration and called it "unfortunate" that the path on tracking apps looked like a particular shape.

Bird is taking it in his stride. He told the BBC he was not angry, only upset about the waste of resources. Whether the crew ever found the car has not been reported. What the flight trackers found is now all over the internet.

headline: Passengers Wait Two Hours for Their Bags, Then They Roll Out Smeared in Brown Goo. The Airline Says It's Not What It Looks Like
dek: Travellers at Atlanta's airport assumed the worst. American Airlines has another explanation, and not everyone is buying it.
location: Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, Georgia, USA
body: American Airlines Flight 2609 from Miami landed in Atlanta at about 8:30 p.m. on Monday, November 16. For the passengers, the flight turned out to be the easy bit.
They say they then spent more than two hours at carousel 8 waiting for their luggage. When it finally came round, dozens of suitcases were coated in a sticky brown substance.

Passenger Derick McCallum filmed the moment for TikTok. The clip captures the crowd recoiling, and one traveller announcing what everyone was thinking: the bags were covered in, to use the technical term, doo-doo.

American Airlines says no. In a statement to Atlanta TV station WSB, the airline said the mess was peanut butter that had leaked out of one passenger's checked bag during the flight and spread onto everyone else's luggage.

The airline apologised and promised to work directly with the affected customers to put things right. In the meantime, passengers were left scrubbing their own suitcases with disinfecting wipes and tissues in the middle of baggage claim.
McCallum is not convinced. His problem is the sheer quantity involved.

body.quote: "How much peanut butter does somebody pack to cover that many bags?" (Derick McCallum, via WSB-TV)

body: Nobody has answered that publicly. Peanut butter is allowed in checked luggage, for what it's worth. The airline has not said whose bag it was, how big the jar was, or whether its owner made it home with enough left for breakfast.

headline: A Three-Legged Earthquake Survivor Wins New York's Dog Mayor Race by 288 Votes. Her Deputy Is Called Dr. Computer Chips
dek: She survived an earthquake, lost a leg and crossed an ocean before winning a 16-candidate race. Then she celebrated with ice cream.
location: Sunnyside, Queens, New York City, USA
body: Move over, Mayor Mamdani. New York City has a second mayor, and she won by 288 votes after a gruelling 15-round contest.
Her name is Machka. She lives in Sunnyside, Queens, she has three legs, and she is an Anatolian Shepherd mix. She is now the city's third Honorary Dog Mayor.

Stephen Calabria, a New York media producer, launched the NYC Dog Mayor election in 2022 as a bit of joy for a city going through hard times. It follows the human political calendar, with a vote every two years. Sixteen dogs enter a March Madness-style bracket and the public votes them through 15 rounds.
In the final, Machka won 4,877 votes. The runner-up, a 13-year-old rescue Shih Tzu who goes by Dr. Computer Chips, got 4,589. In a fine show of bipartisanship, he will serve as Deputy Dog Mayor.

body.h2: A campaign story with real bite

body: Machka's life story would suit any human candidate. She was born on the streets of Elbistan, Turkey, and lost a leg when a car hit her as a puppy. The woman who took her in then lost her home in the 2023 earthquake. Machka eventually reached New York, where Kylen Button adopted her in 2025 through a rescue group.

She ran on an actual platform, too: more pet-friendly housing and homeless shelters. Button, who doubled as campaign manager, says the issue is personal, because many shelters turn away people with pets, which can stop them from getting help.

The official website describes the job as part ambassador and part professional sniffer. Machka is the first dog mayor from Queens, following Sally Long Dog and Simon, a basset and cattle dog mix. Neighbours swarmed her once the result was official, and she marked the win with ice cream. According to Button, Machka would happily campaign for the rest of her life. Her inauguration is set for January 17, 2027.

headline: Scientists Wire Up Monkeys' Brains and Sit Them Down for a Movie Night. The Film They Chose Is Perfect
dek: A serious neuroscience study about how we make sense of what we see needed a test film. The macaques got cartoon chaos, in two languages.
location: City College of New York, New York, USA
body: Watching a film is supposed to be the moment your brain finally clocks off. A new study in the Journal of Neuroscience suggests your brain never got that memo, and it used some unusual moviegoers to prove it.

A team led by Vinay Raghavan at the City College of New York wanted to know how primates pull meaning out of a scene as their eyes dart around it. We don't take in the world in one smooth sweep. Our eyes jump from spot to spot, pausing briefly on each, and the question was what the brain does with all those little glimpses.

First, dozens of people wore EEG caps on their scalps and watched ordinary feature films, including Whiplash and The Big Sick. For a closer look, the team also recorded from electrodes placed inside the brain, in a separate group of human patients and in two female rhesus macaques.
Those deeper recordings needed shorter clips. So the monkeys, sitting in for science, watched ten-minute chunks of Despicable Me. One clip was in English. Another was in Hungarian.
They also watched a short animated film called The Present and three five-minute nature documentaries starring, naturally, other macaques.

The researchers tracked where the viewers looked and matched that with brain activity. They found that when a glimpse brought in genuinely new information about the scene, which they call semantic novelty, it changed activity well beyond the brain's basic visual areas, including regions tied to attention and scene processing. Some of that signal appeared early and fast, between one fixation and the next, as if the brain were predicting what it was about to see.

Their conclusion is that vision works less like a slideshow of separate snapshots and more like a continuous story the brain keeps updating. Raghavan suggested the finding might even help people building AI vision systems.
What it cannot tell us, as 404 Media's Becky Ferreira pointed out, is what a macaque actually thinks of the Minions. Or whether they found them funnier in Hungarian.

headline: Driverless Taxi Spots a Gap Beside a Police Roadblock and Tries to Sneak Through. The Cops Have Other Ideas
dek: Human drivers waited in line. The robot decided it had somewhere better to be. A week later it had a much bigger problem.
location: Interstate 280, San Francisco Bay Area, California, USA
body: On Friday, November 6, the California Highway Patrol was clearing debris from northbound Interstate 280 near John Daly Boulevard in the Bay Area. To protect the crews, officers ran a traffic break, in which patrol cars spread across the lanes and slowly hold everyone behind them.
The human drivers did what humans do. They queued up and waited.

Then a Waymo robotaxi arrived. Instead of joining the line, the driverless car began hunting for a gap next to the police vehicles. Video shared online shows it inching towards an opening, apparently weighing up its chances.
It never got there. A CHP cruiser slid into the gap and shut it. The Waymo backed off into the queue and stayed there like everybody else.

body.quote: "California Highway Patrol Blockade 1, Waymo 0." (Caption from the person who shared the footage, via MotorBiscuit)

body: CHP confirmed the incident to local media. It said the block was improvised on the spot, and that it hadn't been in contact with Waymo or the car's remote operators either before or afterwards. Nobody was ticketed.
The roadblock stunt was not Waymo's only bad freeway week. A day earlier, on November 5, three of its driverless cars drove into an active construction closure on US 101 near Burlingame.

On November 11, California's DMV banned Waymo from offering driverless rides on freeways, calling the repeated wandering into construction zones an "imminent hazard to public safety". Waymo then paused driverless freeway service in every city it serves, including San Francisco, Los Angeles, Miami, Phoenix and Austin. The company says safety is its foundation, that nobody was hurt and nothing was hit, and that its cars are still carrying passengers on ordinary streets. They will just be waiting in line with the rest of us.

headline: Mexico Asks Whether a Pterodactyl Is Flying Over Ciudad Juárez. Experts Say: It Is a Heron
dek: A winged silhouette on a security camera set off dinosaur panic on the border. Officials, scientists and fact-checkers were less excited.
body: Pterosaurs died out about 66 million years ago. This month, a chunk of the internet decided one had turned up in Ciudad Juárez.

Clips of a large winged shape flapping over the city, apparently caught by a surveillance camera near the Anapra area on the border with El Paso, spread fast. Mexico's best-known ufologist, Jaime Maussan, helped promote them.
Comment sections filled with prehistoric theories. Some people were sure they were looking at a living pterodactyl.

Local Civil Protection officials said it was most likely just a large bird. Specialists pointed to the great blue heron, which can have a wingspan of up to about two metres and looks fairly prehistoric when it flaps.
Snopes rated one widely shared clip as fake and said its source was unclear. Other viewers suspected some of the footage was made with AI.

body.quote: Not a dinosaur. Just a very big bird having a very good week.

body: No scientific evidence supports a living pterosaur, in Juárez or anywhere else. The heron has not commented.

headline: A 'Jellyfish UFO' With Tentacles Was Filmed Near an Alaska Air Base. The Leading Theory: A Kite
dek: The internet saw aliens. A UFO filmmaker and a former Pentagon UFO investigator both saw an octopus-shaped show kite.
body: On June 15, photographer Sara Jane Osborn filmed something odd in Anchorage, Alaska: a dark, jellyfish-like object that seemed to hover above a distant tree line, tentacles and all.

After about three minutes, it was gone. The footage resurfaced online in November and took off, helped by one detail: the tree line sits in front of Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, home to F-22 fighter jets.
There is no verified evidence the object entered the base's airspace or had anything to do with the military. That did not slow the alien theories down.

Then the explanations arrived. UFO filmmaker Jeremy Corbell, who has promoted a famous jellyfish-shaped object filmed over Iraq, reportedly concluded on November 11 that this one was most likely a tethered octopus-style show kite.
Former Pentagon UFO investigator Sean Kirkpatrick also reportedly favoured a kite. Other experts suggested high-altitude balloons or military exercises.

body.quote: When the UFO guys say kite, it is probably a kite.

body: Osborn is not convinced. She said she knows the colourful kites flown in Anchorage, though she accepted it might have been a drone-like object. Officially, it remains unidentified.

headline: Family Out Harvesting in Kansas Films a Patchy, Two-Toned Bear. In a State With No Resident Bears
dek: A state biologist confirmed it was a piebald black bear, a genetic oddity he had never seen in Kansas before.
body: Kansas is not bear country. The state's wildlife department says it is not aware of any bears living there year-round.
So a family harvesting their field about 13 miles north of Syracuse, in western Kansas, did a double take when a bear wandered into view. Then they did a triple take, because the bear was patchy.
Instead of the usual solid dark coat, it had blotches of different colours, and the family got it on video.
Matt Peek, a wildlife research biologist with the Kansas Department of Wildlife and Parks, identified it as a piebald black bear, a very rare genetic anomaly that causes the patchy fur.
Peek said it was the first piebald bear he had seen in Kansas, though bears in that part of the state have a history of cinnamon-coloured fur.

body.quote: Rare bear, rarer coat, in a state that barely has bears at all.

body: Almost all confirmed bears in Kansas are yearlings wandering in from neighbouring states after leaving their mothers. This one, it seems, chose to make an entrance.

headline: British Angler Lands a 52kg Carp Called Angelina and Declares Himself a World Record Holder
dek: The fish weighed as much as a small adult. Whether it is officially a world record is a different argument.
body: Most fishing stories involve the one that got away. Ash Hegarty's involves the one that barely fit in the net.
On October 28, the 32-year-old from Blackburn, England, hooked a common carp at Euro Aqua, a private fishing lake near Balatonederics in Hungary. It weighed 114lb 10oz, roughly 52kg.
The fish already had a name: Angelina. Hegarty said she looked like a car tyre in the net.
Hegarty shared the catch on Facebook, calling himself a world record holder, and hundreds of people congratulated him.
Others were less impressed. Critics questioned whether fish from private, well-fed lakes should count, and there has been no confirmed formal international verification of the record.

body.quote: She weighs more than a lot of people reading this. Her name is Angelina.

body: The record books also treat common and mirror carp differently. Angelina is about 800g heavier than a famous 2018 mirror carp, and Euro Aqua has form: a Polish angler caught a 47.4kg carp there in 2024.

headline: Rhode Island Man Grows a 3,156-Pound Pumpkin, the First Ever to Break 3,000
dek: It beat a world record that had stood for exactly one week, by nearly 300 pounds.
body: A small car weighs about 3,000 pounds. Ron Wallace grew a pumpkin that weighs more.
At the Southern New England Giant Pumpkin Weigh Off at Frerichs Farm in Warren, Rhode Island, on October 10, Wallace's pumpkin hit the scale at 3,156 pounds, or 1,431.5kg.
Guinness World Records confirmed it as the heaviest pumpkin ever, and the first in history to pass the 3,000-pound mark.

body.h2: A record that lasted a week

body: The previous record had been set only a week earlier, on October 3, by British grower Ian Paton with a pumpkin of about 2,857 pounds. Wallace beat it by nearly 300.
This is not his first giant. Wallace, 60, set a record in 2006 with a 1,502-pound pumpkin and in 2012 became the first grower to break 2,000 pounds. This is his third world record.

body.quote: One pumpkin. Heavier than a car. Grown on purpose.

body: His secret this year? It was his first season growing in a greenhouse. Guinness called the double record-break 'Pumpkinpalooza'.

headline: Sisters Walk Into Their Airbnb and Find a Framed Photo of Their Own Family on the Wall
dek: The beach print was taken a decade earlier by a stranger with a camera. Commenters say they have seen it in rentals elsewhere too.
body: Vacation rentals are full of generic beach art. Usually it does not include you.

Sisters Libby and Aubrey Birrell, from Utah, were staying at a rental in Oceanside, near San Diego, with about 30 relatives to celebrate their grandfather's 80th birthday when they noticed the big aerial beach print on the wall.
In it were their dad, Libby, and their brother Brady, on a beach outing roughly ten years earlier.
Aubrey posted the discovery on TikTok and it went viral. The host said the home's decorator was a local photographer who takes aerial beach shots and sells them as large prints to vacation rentals.
The sisters think the photo was taken at Mission Beach or Imperial Beach, during a family trip for their brother's soccer tournament. The host offered them a copy.

body.quote: You came for the beach. The beach had already come for you.

body: Not everyone thinks the mystery is fully solved, and the story kicked off a debate about strangers' photos used as decor. Some commenters claimed to have seen the same print in rentals in other states, which has not been confirmed.

headline: A Glowing 'Space Jellyfish' Lights Up the Sky Over Sabah. It Was a Chinese Rocket
dek: Pre-dawn videos of a giant luminous cone spread across Malaysia. The space agency had the answer within a day.
body: Early on Monday, November 9, people in Sabah, Malaysia, looked up and saw something that did not belong in the sky: a huge glowing cone, spreading out like a jellyfish.

Videos from around Kota Kinabalu spread quickly on Threads and other platforms, with the usual theories about aliens and secret aircraft. Similar sightings were reported from Sarawak and the Philippines.
The Malaysian Space Agency, MYSA, said the light came from China's Long March 12 rocket, which launched from Wenchang on Hainan island at 4:24 a.m. Malaysian time.

The effect is known as a space jellyfish. High up, where the air is thin, a rocket's exhaust spreads out widely. The sun, still below the horizon for people on the ground, lights up the plume from below, so it glows against a dark sky.

body.quote: Not an alien. Just physics, exhaust and very good timing.

body: It is the same trick that has produced UFO panics around the world after launches. It is also, admittedly, a much better photo than most rockets manage.

headline: Airport Staff Notice Socks Are Moving. Inside: More Than 3,000 Tarantulas
dek: Three travellers tried to fly from Lima to Europe with a suitcase zoo of eggs, babies and adult spiders stuffed into dirty socks.
body: Most people pack socks to wear them. Three travellers at Lima's Jorge Chávez International Airport packed socks to hide tarantulas in them. More than 3,000 of them.
Acting on an anonymous tip, officers stopped the group, two German citizens and one Polish citizen, as they were checking in for a flight to Europe in early November 2026.
Inside three suitcases were dozens of socks, and inside the socks were tarantulas at every stage of life: eggs, juveniles and fully grown adults.
Peru's National Forest and Wildlife Service, SERFOR, said the spiders were bound for Germany, where exotic tarantulas are prized by collectors.
One outlet estimated a single tarantula can fetch around 500 euros in Europe, which would put the sock collection at roughly 1.5 million euros. That figure has not been officially confirmed.

body.quote: Somewhere in Germany, a collector is still waiting for a very hairy delivery.

body: The three were handed to prosecutors. In Peru, wildlife trafficking can mean three to five years in prison, rising to seven when protected species are involved. Socks are a recurring theme: Lima officers caught a man with hundreds of tarantulas strapped to his body in 2024.

headline: Nine-Year-Old Uses AI to Put a Python in the Toilet. Police Search for Two Days
dek: Firefighters and police in a small Italian town hunted for a snake that only ever existed on a phone.
body: On November 12, a family in Castelfidardo, a hill town near Ancona in central Italy, called for help. They had a photo of what looked like a royal python poking its head out of their toilet.
Police and firefighters took it seriously. Nobody wants a python loose in the plumbing, so the search began.
It went on for two days. The snake never showed up, because the snake had never existed.
The photo had been made by the family's nine-year-old son with an artificial intelligence app. Officers only worked it out after examining the original image on his phone.
The boy owned up and, according to one report, apologised to the officers. Which app he used has not been reported.

body.quote: Two days, a fire crew and a police unit versus one bored kid. The kid won.

body: One photography site noted that an AI image detector rated the fake snake as authentic, which says something about how good the tools have become. Castelfidardo's toilets, meanwhile, remain python-free.

headline: Woman Empties a Halloween Candy Bowl on Camera, Gets Fired for Lying About Saying Sorry
dek: She was wearing her work shirt. Her sushi restaurant boss was more upset about the fake apology than the candy.
body: Leaving out a bowl of candy on Halloween is an act of trust. In Helena, Alabama, a doorbell camera showed that trust being scooped up by the handful.
The video shows two adult women at an unattended candy bowl. One of them took nearly everything in it, while wearing a shirt from Sakana Sushi Bar & Grill.
The clip spread on Facebook, and the internet did what it does: it read the shirt.

body.h2: The cover-up was worse than the crime

body: The restaurant confirmed that the woman was an off-duty employee. At first, it said she had gone back, returned the candy and apologised.
The homeowner disagreed. He said the only apology he got came from the other woman in the video. Sakana then said it had confirmed the employee lied about apologising, and fired her.

body.quote: Taking candy from children: bad. Lying to your boss about it: unemployment.

body: The restaurant said it does not condone taking from children or hurting the community. Alabama is an at-will employment state, so the candy may end up being the most expensive she ever ate.

headline: Man Drives to Police Station at 2 a.m. to Report Lost Phone, Fails Breath Test in the Parking Lot
dek: Officers noticed his truck before they noticed his complaint. It was on the sidewalk.
body: Losing your phone after a night out is annoying. Reporting it to the police is reasonable. Driving there yourself, at 2 a.m., after the bar, is where this story turns.
A 42-year-old man showed up at Abbotsford Police headquarters in British Columbia to report that his phone had gone missing after he left a bar in an Uber.
Before he could get far with the paperwork, a patrol officer spotted his truck being driven on the sidewalk inside the station's own parking lot.

body.h2: Wrong place, wrong time, wrong everything

body: Officers gave him a breath test. He failed it.
He was handed a 90-day driving ban and his vehicle was impounded. The Abbotsford Police Department shared the story on social media, where it did considerably better than his night.

body.quote: He took an Uber home from the bar. Then he drove to the police.

body: There is no word on whether the phone was ever found. If it was, he will need to get a ride to pick it up.

headline: Woman Reaches Over the Side of a Boat to Pet a Great White Shark. The Shark Has Other Ideas
dek: A tagging trip off Georgia produced a viral clip of an apex predator swinging round at a hand that should not have been there.
body: There are animals you pet, and there are animals you photograph from a respectful distance. The great white shark is firmly in the second group.
Off Tybee Island, Georgia, a guest on a research trip with the Knot Lucky White Shark Tagging Program reached over the side of the boat toward a great white swimming alongside.
The shark thrashed, swung round and lunged toward her. She pulled her hand back just in time, and she was not hurt.

body.h2: The crew says it was under control

body: The guest, a military veteran named Jen, was on the trip as part of the program. Founder Jimmy Armel said she was never in real danger, because the crew had the shark under control the whole time.
Not everyone was reassured. University of Sydney shark researcher Chris Pepin-Neff criticised the attempt to touch the animal.

body.quote: The shark was not tagged. The lesson, hopefully, was.

body: The shark itself could not be tagged because of safety concerns for the crew and the animal. It swam off having made its position on petting very clear.

headline: Police Turn a Real Car Chase Into a GTA Video and Tell the Driver He Should Have Waited for GTA 6
dek: Derbyshire officers added wanted stars, a minimap and a soundtrack. The driver gets to enjoy the game's launch from a cell.
body: Police social media teams have discovered the most powerful weapon in law enforcement: video editing.

On November 3, Derbyshire Police posted a TikTok of officers chasing a black van, restyled to look like Grand Theft Auto. The clip came with a wanted-star display, a tiny map tracking the van and a dramatic soundtrack.
The caption suggested the driver could simply have waited a few more weeks and done his driving in GTA 6 instead.
Police said the 28-year-old driver was arrested for dangerous driving, driving while disqualified, drug-driving and possessing cannabis. The chase reportedly took place in Ripley.
Reports say he was jailed for 14 months, which means he will miss the real game's release.

body.quote: Gamers spotted the HUD showed five wanted stars. GTA 6 has six.

body: Viewers being viewers, the main complaint online was not about the driving. It was about the star count, and whether the police got the game details right.

headline: Thief Steals Five Cars From Dealership, Stops to Eat Candy and Spray the Owner's Cologne
dek: He took a Porsche and a BMW with the For Sale sticker still on it. The BMW's tracker led police to his front door.
body: Some thieves are in and out in minutes. Others treat the crime scene like a spa day.

Police in South Florida say 35-year-old Michael Guevara broke into Cabrera's Auto, a dealership in Hialeah Gardens, early on a Sunday morning using a crowbar and a claw hammer. Surveillance video shows him scouting the area first.
Once inside, he grabbed the key fobs and helped himself to five cars worth more than $200,000, including a 2019 Porsche Macan.
He also found time to eat candy, leaving the wrappers in a BMW, and to spray himself with the owner's cologne.
He drove the cars to various spots and took the BMW home. That was the mistake: police used the car's tracking system to find it at his house, still wearing its For Sale decal.

body.quote: He smelled great. That is about where the good news ended.

body: Officers arrested him at gunpoint. He faces burglary, five counts of grand theft and possession of burglary tools, and a judge denied him house arrest. The owner said all five cars were recovered undamaged.

headline: Woman Feeds Her Dogs Invisible Treats. One Catches On. The Other Is Still Chewing
dek: Xena figured it out by round two and walked away. Luna kept happily eating nothing.
body: Not every viral story needs a crime. Some just need a dog with total faith in humanity.
In a YouTube Short that spread this week, a woman gives her two dogs, Xena and Luna, a real treat. Then she quietly switches to pretend ones to see how long it takes them to notice.
At first, both dogs happily accept the imaginary snacks.
By the second round, Xena has worked it out. She gives her owner a look and walks off.
Luna does not walk off. Luna keeps taking every invisible treat offered, chewing and swallowing with complete commitment.

body.quote: Xena wants a treat. Luna simply enjoys the idea of one.

body: Commenters agreed that Luna is living her best life, and that the real treat is never questioning anything. The clip was posted by the account @heymynamesluna.

headline: Golden Toilet Thief Admits He Used the £4.75m Loo the Day Before It Vanished. His Review: Splendid
dek: An 18-carat gold toilet was ripped out of Winston Churchill's birthplace in five minutes. It has never been seen again.
body: It was called America. It was a fully working toilet made of solid 18-carat gold, weighing about 98 kilograms and insured for £4.75 million. And one day it was simply gone.

The toilet, created by Italian artist Maurizio Cattelan, was plumbed in and ready for use as part of an exhibition at Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire, the birthplace of Winston Churchill. Visitors could book a slot and use it.

Before dawn on September 14, 2019, a gang rammed two stolen vehicles through the palace's locked wooden gates, smashed through a window and a door, and tore the toilet out of the floor. The whole raid took about five minutes.

At the trial in 2025, one 39-year-old defendant admitted he had visited the palace the day before the heist and used the golden toilet. Asked in court what the experience was like, he gave a one-word review.

body.quote: "Splendid."

body: His phone told a less innocent story. It held photos of the toilet, a selfie with it, a picture of the cubicle lock, and the very window later smashed in the raid. He claimed he had been photographing flags in the distance and simply thought the lock was funny.

The jury was not convinced, and he was convicted of burglary. The ringleader, who had pleaded guilty, got four more years on top of a near 20-year sentence for other crimes. The man who called it splendid got 27 months. The judge called the heist bold and brazen.
None of the gold has ever been found. Prosecutors believe it was cut up and sold, which means somewhere out there, someone may be wearing jewellery made from a toilet.

headline: Bank Accidentally Puts $81 Trillion Into a Customer's Account Instead of $280
dek: One employee typed it. A second checked it. Neither noticed the extra 11 zeros.
body: Everyone has made a typo at work. Few have made one worth almost three times the entire US economy.

In April 2024, Citigroup credited a customer account with $81 trillion. The amount was supposed to be $280. The Financial Times revealed the blunder in February 2025, and other outlets including CBS News followed up.

Here is the part that makes it truly special. The payment was entered by one employee and then reviewed by a second. Neither spotted the problem, and the transaction was approved to go through the next day.
About 90 minutes after it posted, a third employee noticed something slightly off about an $81 trillion balance. The transaction was reversed a few hours later.

Citi said no money ever actually left the bank, describing the cause as an inputting error between two of its own internal ledger accounts. It reported the incident to US regulators as a near miss, the term for a wrong payment that gets caught and recovered.

body.quote: According to an internal report cited by the FT, Citi had 10 near misses of $1 billion or more in 2024. That was an improvement on the year before.

body: For perspective, the entire US economy produced about $29 trillion in 2024. For a few hours, one account at Citi held nearly three of them.

headline: Raccoon Breaks Into Liquor Store, Drinks the Scotch Shelf Dry, Passes Out in the Bathroom
dek: Staff opened up on Saturday morning to smashed bottles, a whisky lake on the floor and one very unconscious masked burglar.
body: Some people end a long week at the bar. One raccoon in Virginia decided to skip the bar entirely and go straight to the warehouse.

Overnight into Saturday, November 29, the animal broke into a closed, state-run Virginia ABC liquor store near Ashland in Hanover County. Investigators believe it came in through the roof: a ceiling tile gave way, and the raccoon came down with it.

What happened next was less a burglary and more a bender. The raccoon headed straight for the bottom shelf, home of the scotch and whisky, and started knocking bottles over. Glass shattered. Liquor pooled across the floor. Security cameras captured the aftermath, which looked roughly like a frat party with fewer witnesses.

body.quote: The county's animal control officer said the raccoon had drunk nearly everything it could reach.

body: When an employee arrived the next morning, the culprit was not hiding or fleeing. It was lying flat out on the bathroom floor, completely unconscious.

Hanover County Animal Protection and Shelter collected the suspect and, in a rare act of mercy toward a burglar, simply let it sleep it off. After a few hours of rest it had no injuries at all, except what staff described as a probable hangover.

The shelter later joked online about the raccoon's poor life choices and said it hoped the animal had learned that breaking and entering is wrong. Once sober, the raccoon was released back into the wild with no charges filed and, presumably, a pounding headache.

headline: Hundreds of Timothée Chalamet Clones Swarm a NYC Park, Cops Shut It Down, Then the Real Timothée Shows Up
dek: The prize was $50. The crowd was enormous. The police were not amused. The actor himself was.
body: It started as a joke. It ended with police, handcuffs, a $500 fine and the arrival of the one man nobody expected to see.

On Sunday, October 27, 2024, a YouTube personality hosted a Timothée Chalamet look-alike contest near Washington Square Park in Manhattan. The prize was a modest $50. Flyers went up around the city, an online invite collected thousands of RSVPs, and hundreds of people turned out to watch.
The contestants came prepared. There were curly-haired Willy Wonkas, desert-ready Dune heroes and a great many sharp cheekbones.

Just as the look-alikes started walking a red carpet, police ordered the crowd to break up. Organisers were fined $500 for holding an unpermitted costume contest, and at least one contestant was led away in handcuffs.

body.quote: Then, out of nowhere, the real Timothée Chalamet walked in, flanked by bodyguards, and posed for photos with his doppelgängers.

body: Undeterred, the contest moved to a nearby playground. More than a dozen hopefuls took to a makeshift stage, and four finalists were quizzed on their French, their plans to improve the world and their intentions toward Kylie Jenner.

The winner, a 21-year-old from Staten Island in a purple Wonka outfit who threw candy from a briefcase, walked away with a novelty cheque made out to Best Tim. One of the producers summed it up: what began as a silly joke turned into total pandemonium.

headline: Cops Disguise Themselves as a Dancing Lion to Pounce on Burglar Who Robbed a Police Chief 3 Times
dek: He always ran when he saw officers. He did not run from a giant papier-mache lion at a temple fair.
body: Thai police had a problem. Their suspect, a serial burglar, had a simple strategy: every time he spotted an officer, he ran. So the officers stopped looking like officers. They started looking like a lion.

The man was accused of breaking into the Bangkok home of a local police commander not once, not twice, but three times in early February 2026. The haul was worth about 2 million baht, roughly $64,000, and included Buddhist amulets and artifacts, among them two foot-tall Buddha statues.

Investigators followed the trail of stolen amulets he had sold and learned he liked to visit temples in Nonthaburi province, on the edge of Bangkok. After weeks of surveillance, they came up with a plan worthy of a heist movie.

On February 18, at a Lunar New Year temple fair, plainclothes officers joined a lion dance procession hidden inside a red-and-yellow lion costume. As the 33-year-old suspect wandered through the festivities, the lion slowly danced its way toward him.

body.quote: Then the officer holding the lion's head lunged, and the lion pinned the burglar to the ground.

body: Colleagues rushed in to help, and Thailand's Metropolitan Police Bureau proudly released photos and video of what may be the most festive arrest in history.
Police said the man confessed and told them he stole to fund gambling and drugs. He already had prior convictions for theft. He also, presumably, now has a lifelong fear of parades.

headline: Japan Now Sells a Washing Machine for Humans, and Its Maker Says It Cleans Your Soul
dek: You lie in a pod, close the lid and get washed like a load of laundry. It costs about $385,000.
body: Showers are fine. Baths are nice. But have you ever wanted to be washed exactly like a pair of socks? Japan has you covered.

In late November 2025, the Osaka company Science Co. began selling its Mirai Ningen Sentakki, which translates as Future Human Washing Machine. You lie down inside a pod, close the lid, and it cleans you the way a washing machine cleans clothes. There is, thankfully, no spin cycle.
While you soak, music plays and the machine monitors your heartbeat and other vital signs. A company spokesperson told AFP that it washes not only your body but also your soul.

body.h2: From Expo novelty to real product

body: A prototype was one of the hits of Expo 2025 in Osaka, which drew more than 27 million visitors. Demand to try it was so high that people had to win a lottery for a turn.
The idea is not new. It is an update of a human-washing machine shown at the last Osaka Expo in 1970, which inspired the company's president when he was ten years old.

body.quote: The company only decided to make it for real after a US resort company asked whether it would ever be sold.

body: Only about 50 units are planned, at a reported price of around ¥60 million, or roughly $385,000 each. An Osaka hotel bought the first one and rents it out in a private spa room, and an electronics chain ordered another to lure shoppers into its stores. Each wash takes about 20 minutes and includes bubbles and a warm mist. Detergent, presumably, is optional.

headline: Beavers Finish Government's 7-Year Dam Project Overnight, Save Taxpayers $1.2 Million
dek: Officials spent years on permits and land talks. A family of rodents spent a couple of nights on it and did a better job.
location: Brdy Protected Landscape Area, Czech Republic
body: Every government has a project that seems to take forever. In the Czech Republic, one of them was finally finished, and not by anyone on the payroll.

Conservation officials had wanted to build barriers near the Klabava River, on a former army training ground south-west of Prague that became a protected area in 2016. The goal was to shield the river, and its critically endangered crayfish, from sediment and acidic water draining out of two nearby ponds, and to create a wetland along the way.

The plan was drawn up in 2018. It was approved. It had a budget of about 30 million koruna, roughly $1.2 million. And then it sat there for years, stuck in negotiations over land and permits between military forest managers and the river basin authority.

Before a single excavator arrived, a local beaver family of around eight animals took matters into their own paws. They built at least four dams across a drainage gully soldiers had once dug, with more under construction.

The resulting network of pools and channels covers about twice the area the human planners had in mind. The head of the protected-area administration said the beavers had created the habitat almost overnight, with no paperwork and at no cost, saving the state the entire 30 million crowns.

body.quote: A zoologist pointed out the key difference: beavers can build a dam in a night or two, while people need permits and funding first.

body: Officials said they do not expect any conflict with their new unpaid contractors for at least a decade. The nearest farmland that could be affected is far from the site. The beavers have not submitted an invoice.

headline: Thieves Steal 12 Tonnes of KitKats, All 413,793 Bars, and Vanish Without a Trace
dek: Nestlé says the criminals took its slogan too literally. The chocolate is still out there.
body: For decades, KitKat has told the world to have a break. Somewhere in Europe, a gang of thieves decided to have 413,793 of them.

Nestlé announced that a truck carrying about 12 tonnes of KitKat bars had been stolen on its way from the company's production site in central Italy to Poland. The chocolate was meant for shops across Europe. It never arrived.
To make it even more absurd, the stolen bars came from KitKat's new Formula 1 range, shaped like tiny racing cars. The thieves made a clean getaway, which feels appropriate.

body.quote: In its statement, KitKat said the criminals had taken its famous slogan too literally, and praised their exceptional taste.

body: When the company went public, neither the truck nor its sweet cargo had been found, and no arrests had been reported. Nobody was hurt.

Nestlé has turned every chocolate fan into a detective. Each bar carries a batch code, and shoppers, shops and wholesalers can scan it to see whether their snack is from the stolen load. If it matches, they get instructions for alerting the company.

The company said the bars are perfectly safe to eat and that it was going public to highlight a real problem: cargo theft is on the rise for businesses of every size. Somewhere, someone is sitting on half a million chocolate racing cars and wondering what to do next.

headline: Spain Orders €258 Million of New Trains, Then Finds Out They Won't Fit Through the Tunnels
dek: Someone got the measurements wrong. Two of the country's top transport officials lost their jobs.
body: Measure twice, cut once. It is advice every carpenter knows, and apparently advice nobody passed on to Spain's railways.

In June 2020, Renfe, Spain's state rail operator, ordered 31 new commuter trains worth about €258 million from the Spanish manufacturer CAF. They were meant for the narrow-gauge lines that wind through the mountains of Asturias and Cantabria in the north of the country.

There was just one problem. The measurements CAF had been given were wrong. In March 2021, the manufacturer realised the trains would be too wide to pass through some of the tunnels on the route, and stopped building.
The tunnels in question were dug in the 1800s, and their dimensions do not match modern standards. Somewhere between the old tunnels and the new trains, nobody checked.

When the story finally became public in February 2023, the fallout was swift. The president of Renfe and Spain's secretary of state for transport both resigned, after two senior rail officials had already been fired.

body.quote: Cantabria's regional president called it a monumental botch, demanded that heads roll, and asked for compensation.

body: The government and Renfe insisted no money had been wasted because the error was caught before any trains were built. Delivery of the new trains slipped from 2024 to 2026, and rail officials launched an inquiry into how a nine-figure order ended up depending on the wrong tape measure.

headline: Godzilla Egg? Giant Mystery Metal Ball Washes Up on Japanese Beach and the Bomb Squad Is Called In
dek: The internet guessed bombs, UFOs and kaiju. An oceanographer took one look and solved it.
body: When a giant metal sphere appears on your beach, you have two options. Ignore it, or call the bomb squad. Japan chose the bomb squad.

In February 2023, a hollow iron ball almost 1.5 metres wide was discovered on a beach in Hamamatsu, south-west of Tokyo. A local jogger told the broadcaster NHK it had been sitting there for about a month, and that it would not move when he pushed it.

Police sealed off the beach and sent in explosives experts. X-rays showed the ball was hollow and not dangerous, but officials did not say what it actually was. The internet was happy to fill the gap.
Social media users dubbed it a Godzilla egg. Other theories included a bomb, an alien craft and something from outer space. It did not help that Japan was already on edge over suspected spy balloons.

The city eventually concluded it was most likely a foreign-made buoy. An oceanographer in Scotland agreed, telling the BBC he recognised it immediately as the kind of float used to hold ocean instruments.

body.quote: He explained that such buoys can drift for decades and lose their markings, and look a lot like old sea mines, minus the spikes.

body: Within days, a heavy lifting machine hauled the ball away to be stored and later disposed of. One official said they were relieved it was finally gone. Godzilla, as far as we know, has not come looking for it.

headline: Court Rules a Fart Is Not Free Speech After Man Deliberately Lets One Rip at Police
dek: He was fined €500. He appealed on free-expression grounds. The judge was not moved.
body: Some legal battles define a nation's values. This one was about a fart.

On June 5, 2020, police in a Vienna park stopped a man sitting on a bench with friends for a routine ID check. According to police, he rose slightly from the bench, looked the officers straight in the eye, and released what they described as a massive fart.

Vienna police fined him €500 for offending public decency. They explained on Twitter that nobody gets fined for an accidental toot, but this man had already been provocative and uncooperative earlier that day. They added, drily, that their officers do not much enjoy being farted at.

The man fought the fine. In April 2021, Vienna's administrative court reduced it to €100 because of his clean record and finances. But the judge firmly rejected his argument that the fart was a protected form of expression.

body.quote: Farts and burps, the ruling said, have no communicative content, and even if they did, they would go beyond the bounds of decency.

body: The court record described in loving detail how he lifted his buttocks before letting go, while his friends laughed and he grinned at the officers.

His lawyer insisted it was either unintentional or free speech, and vowed to take the matter all the way to Austria's Constitutional Court on principle. The rest of us are left to wonder what the founding fathers of Austrian law would have made of it.

headline: Man Accused of Swapping $34,000 of LEGO for Pasta. Police Say His Plan Got Cooked Al Dente
dek: He allegedly bought LEGO sets, kept the pieces, filled the boxes with dried pasta and returned them. At least 70 times.
body: Some people build LEGO. One man allegedly built a pasta-based retail scheme so elaborate it deserves its own instruction booklet.

Police in Irvine, California, arrested a 28-year-old man from nearby Paramount on suspicion of grand theft. According to investigators, his method was simple. Buy expensive LEGO sets at Target. Take out the minifigures and valuable pieces. Fill the boxes back up with dried pasta so they weigh about the same. Return them for a full refund.
Police say he pulled it off at least 70 times at Target stores across the country, racking up around $34,000 in losses.
Irvine detectives eventually set up surveillance at a local Target, identified their man and arrested him at the store, all captured on officers' body cameras.
The department then released photos of the recovered evidence: piles of LEGO figures, including Star Wars characters, alongside bags of durum wheat semolina pasta allegedly used as stand-ins.

body.quote: On Facebook, police called it a bad build and warned that any master plan swapping LEGOs for linguine will end up cooked al dente.

body: He was booked into Orange County Jail. Target has not said whether it plans to start weighing its returns more carefully, or simply start checking them for spaghetti.

headline: Astronaut Accused of Secretly Eating a Space Tomato Is Cleared When It Turns Up 8 Months Later
dek: It floated away on the International Space Station. Everyone assumed he ate it. He didn't.
body: It is one of the great mysteries of modern spaceflight. Not dark matter. Not black holes. A missing tomato.

NASA astronaut Frank Rubio harvested a tiny tomato grown aboard the International Space Station, put it in a bag, and took it out to show some students. He thought he had velcroed it back in place afterwards. He had not. It floated off into the station and vanished.

Rubio spent 18 to 20 hours searching for it without success and concluded it had probably dried out beyond recognition. His crewmates, and much of the internet, had a different theory: he ate it. He denied this.

Rubio went on to spend more than a year in space, a record for an American astronaut, after a problem with his Soyuz spacecraft doubled his planned stay. He returned to Earth with the tomato question still hanging over him.
Then, on December 6, 2023, during a livestream for the station's 25th anniversary, astronaut Jasmin Moghbeli announced that the crew had found it.

body.quote: Moghbeli told viewers the crew could finally exonerate their former crewmate.

body: NASA later revealed there were actually two lost tomatoes, found together in a plastic bag, dehydrated and slightly squished but free of visible mould. The station is bigger than a six-bedroom house, which leaves plenty of corners for fruit to hide. The famous tomatoes were thrown away rather than brought home, ending their journey with no honours at all.

headline: World's Best Chess Player Gets Kicked Out of World Championship for Wearing Jeans. The Jeans Then Sell for $36,100
dek: He refused to change. Officials refused to budge. Then they changed the rules and he came back.
body: Chess is a game of strategy, patience and, it turns out, trousers.

In December 2024, world number one Magnus Carlsen arrived at the FIDE World Rapid and Blitz Championships in New York wearing a shirt, a blazer and jeans. He said he had come straight from a lunch meeting. The tournament's dress code explicitly banned jeans.

Officials fined him $200 and told him to change. Carlsen offered to change the next day. Officials said now. He refused, calling it a matter of principle, and was left out of the next round's pairings, which meant he was out of the event.
Chess's governing body said the rule applied equally to everyone, pointing out that another grandmaster had been fined the same day for wearing sports shoes and had simply gone and changed.

Carlsen at first said he was done with the whole thing and joked he would head somewhere with better weather. Then FIDE relaxed its ban on jeans, and he came back for the blitz event. He made the final, and after three drawn sudden-death games he and his opponent agreed to share the title, a first for an over-the-board world championship.

body.quote: The jeans themselves went on eBay a few months later and sold for $36,100, with the money going to charity.

body: Bidding sat at $14,100 for days before 29 bids in under half an hour sent the price soaring. The buyer also paid $74 for shipping, which feels like the most reasonable part of the entire story.

headline: Couple Accidentally Mails Their Cat to Amazon in a Box of Boots. She Survives 6 Days and 600 Miles
dek: The returns warehouse opened the package expecting steel-toed boots. It found a calico instead.
location: Lehi, Utah to Jurupa Valley, California, USA
body: Every cat owner knows cats love boxes. One family in Utah learned exactly how far that love can take a cat: about 630 miles.

On April 10, 2024, a man in Lehi, Utah, packed five pairs of steel-toed work boots back into a large box to return them to Amazon. What he did not notice was Galena, the family's six-year-old indoor calico and a well-known box enthusiast, who had quietly climbed in with them.
The box was sealed and shipped. The family spent the next week searching for their cat, putting up posters and posting appeals on social media, with no idea she was riding UPS across state lines.

On April 16, a worker at an Amazon returns warehouse in Jurupa Valley, California, opened the box and found a cat where the boots should have been. An off-duty employee who rescues cats on the side came in with food and a carrier and took her home.

Galena had spent roughly six days in the box with no food or water. A vet found her a little thinner and mildly dehydrated but otherwise fine, with normal bloodwork. Her microchip led the vet straight to her owners, who at first assumed the phone call was a prank.

body.quote: The owners credited three small miracles: a split seam that let in air, mild weather, and the warehouse worker who took her in.

body: The couple flew to California for the reunion, then drove about ten hours home with Galena. Their advice to other pet owners: get your pets microchipped, and triple-check your Amazon boxes.

headline: Officials Beg Fans to Respect the Privacy of Neil, a 1-Ton Seal Who Fights Parked Cars
dek: He bends bollards, smashes barriers and lies in the road. He also has more TikTok followers than Tasmania has people.
body: Most celebrities ask for privacy after a scandal. Neil has had a dozen scandals, and he is a seal, so officials are asking on his behalf.

Neil is a five-year-old male southern elephant seal weighing around 1,000 kilograms, about as much as a small car. Twice a year, after months of feeding at sea, he hauls himself ashore for a tour of beachside towns in southern Tasmania. His latest visit was his twelfth.
His TikTok following of 1.4 million is more than double Tasmania's entire human population. His criminal record is similarly impressive.

Over his visits, Neil has bent traffic bollards, damaged a sign warning the public about seals, flattened a fence he tried to vault, picked fights with parked cars and smashed through barriers built specifically to keep him off the roads. He enjoys lying in the middle of the street, occasionally bringing an entire town to a halt, and keeps returning to a favourite sidewalk puddle even after rangers relocate him.

At a news conference in Hobart, a state wildlife official asked fans to give Neil some space, calling his fame a double-edged sword. He warned that people risk loving Neil to death, and asked the public to stop revealing which town the seal is currently in.

body.quote: A seal scientist explained that young males practise for adult dominance battles. With no rivals around, Neil practises on cars.

body: Some fans online have embraced him as an anti-authority hero. A local resident called him one of the area's biggest exports. If he reaches adulthood, Neil could grow to about five metres long and triple his weight, which is bad news for the bollards.

headline: Man Hollows Out a 1,214-Pound Pumpkin and Paddles It 46 Miles Down a River for a World Record
dek: He named it Punky Loafster. It nearly sank. He paddled through the night anyway.
location: Columbia River, Washington and Oregon, USA
body: Cinderella turned a pumpkin into a carriage. One Oregon man turned his into a boat and set off down one of America's biggest rivers.

The 46-year-old giant-pumpkin grower from Happy Valley, Oregon, raised a 1,214-pound monster he named Punky Loafster. He pollinated it in July, harvested it in early October, and a week later carved it into a vessel.

On October 12 and 13, 2024, he paddled it 73.5 kilometres, about 46 miles, down the Columbia River from North Bonneville to Vancouver, Washington. The trip took roughly 26 hours over three legs and smashed the previous Guinness record of 63 kilometres.

He wrote the words it's real on both sides of his pumpkin so people watching from the shore would not think it was a prop. Winds of around 35 mph sent waves crashing over the sides, and the pumpkin began taking on water.

At a stop near Multnomah Falls, he lightened his boat by scooping out more pumpkin flesh with a soup can. He then paddled through the night, because pulling up on a rocky beach risked puncturing the hull.

body.quote: Kayakers and a pontoon boat followed him the whole way, just in case the pumpkin gave up before he did.

body: He has been growing giant pumpkins since 2011 and racing them in a local pumpkin regatta since 2013, which raises the question of how many other people are out there quietly training for this.

headline: Man Spends 8 Years Gluing 706,000 Matchsticks Into a Giant Eiffel Tower. Guinness Says He Used the Wrong Matches
dek: The record was rejected over a technicality. Then the internet got angry and Guinness backed down.
body: Some people build model ships in bottles. One Frenchman built an Eiffel Tower taller than a two-storey house, out of matchsticks.

The 47-year-old spent eight years and about 4,200 hours on his creation, a 1:45 scale replica standing 7.19 metres tall. It used more than 706,000 matchsticks and 23 kilograms of glue. He placed the final match on December 27, 2023.

Early on, he cut the flammable heads off ordinary matches by hand. When that became too tedious, he started ordering plain wooden sticks without heads directly from a French match manufacturer. That decision would come back to haunt him.
In late January 2024, Guinness World Records turned down his record attempt. The reason: his sticks were not commercially available matches.
He told French television the rejection had really hurt. The public agreed it was absurd, and after a wave of criticism, Guinness reversed its decision.

body.quote: A Guinness records director admitted the organisation had been heavy-handed and said it regretted the distress it had caused.

body: Guinness also rewrote its rules so that future builders can cut and shape their matchsticks however they like. The Frenchman's tower officially beat the previous record of 6.53 metres, set in 2009. He even hired a survey company to confirm the height, just in case anyone else had questions.

headline: Steel Conker Scandal: 82-Year-Old King Conker Accused of Cheating With a Metal Chestnut
dek: His opponent's conker shattered in one hit. Then a steel one turned up in the champion's pocket.
body: Every sport has its doping scandal. The World Conker Championships have a steel chestnut.

More than 200 people entered the 2024 championships, held on October 13 at a pub in the English village of Southwick. The rules are simple: thread a horse chestnut onto a string, take turns whacking your opponent's conker, and try to smash it.

The men's title went to an 82-year-old veteran known to everyone as King Conker. His opponent in the final was less than thrilled, and raised the alarm after his own conker exploded in a single strike.
Organisers confirmed that a steel conker had been found in the champion's pocket. He denied any wrongdoing.

The committee investigated, reviewing photos, video and statements from judges and umpires. On October 21 they cleared him, accepting that he carried the metal conker purely to amuse people as part of his King Conker persona.

body.quote: The committee's chair said four judges had watched him so closely that cheating was absolutely impossible.

body: The beaten finalist accepted the verdict gracefully. And in the end, King Conker did not take the overall crown anyway. That went to a 34-year-old woman from Indianapolis, who beat him to become the first American champion since the contest began in 1965.

headline: Museum's Beer-Can Artwork Thrown in the Bin by a Worker Who Thought It Was Litter
dek: The cans were hand-painted masterpieces. The new lift engineer saw two empty beers and did the tidy thing.
body: Modern art is often accused of looking like rubbish. At one Dutch museum, someone took that literally.

The LAM museum in Lisse was displaying a work by French artist Alexandre Lavet called All The Good Times We Spent Together. It appears to be two empty, dented beer cans. In fact, they are meticulously hand-painted with acrylics, a piece the museum says took enormous time and effort.
To surprise visitors, the museum placed the cans in its glass lift shaft, as though someone had carelessly left them behind. The illusion worked a little too well.
A lift engineer who had just started working at the museum spotted the cans, decided they were trash, and threw them away.
A curator returning from a short break noticed the artwork was gone and found it in a bin bag full of swept-up litter, just before it was taken away for good. Both cans survived intact.

body.quote: A museum spokesperson said there were no hard feelings, and that the engineer was only doing his job.

body: The cans were cleaned up and moved to a traditional plinth so the artwork could rest after its adventure. The museum's director said the whole point of the collection is to make people look at everyday objects in a new way. Mission, arguably, accomplished.

headline: Orcas Bring Back 1987's Hottest Fashion Trend: Wearing Dead Salmon as Hats
dek: A killer whale was photographed with a fish balanced on its head, reviving a mystery that has baffled scientists for nearly 40 years.
body: Fashion is cyclical, and apparently that applies to killer whales too.

On October 25, 2024, a photographer near Point No Point in Puget Sound captured a male orca swimming along with a dead salmon perched neatly on top of his head. The nonprofit Orca Network reported the sighting, and researchers identified the whale as J27, nicknamed Blackberry, a 32-year-old male from J pod.
J pod belongs to the endangered southern resident killer whales, a population of about 71 animals split into three pods that eat nothing but fish. And they have a history with this particular look.

body.h2: The summer of the salmon hat

body: In 1987, a female in K pod started wearing salmon on her head. Within months, the trend had spread to the other two pods. Then, almost as suddenly as it began, it vanished, and it was barely seen again for decades.

The new sighting came during an unusually big chum salmon run, the same week J pod spent a rare ten days in a row being spotted in the area. That may matter, because nobody actually knows why orcas do this. Theories include playing with spare food, saving a snack for later, or some kind of social food-sharing.

body.quote: One biologist summed up the science honestly: it is all speculation.

body: She has seen southern residents wear the look four or five times since 2005, and says it at least suggests a whale with plenty to eat. Other experts are not ready to call a full comeback. One photo, they note, does not make a trend. Fashion critics in the Pacific Northwest remain divided.

headline: Man Lives 120 Days in a Steel Capsule at the Bottom of the Sea, Then Pops Up for Champagne and a Cigar
dek: No shower, four cameras and a copy of Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea by the bed.
location: Off the Caribbean coast of Panama
body: Most people find a week of working from home isolating. One man spent four months working from the bottom of the ocean.
On January 24, 2025, a 59-year-old German aerospace engineer climbed out of a capsule submerged 11 metres below the surface off Panama's Caribbean coast. He had been living inside it for 120 days.

His underwater home measured about 30 square metres and was connected by a tube with a narrow spiral staircase to a chamber above the waves, where food, visitors and a doctor could reach him. Inside he had a bed, a toilet, a TV, a computer, internet and an exercise bike. What he did not have was a shower.
Four cameras recorded his every move, both to keep an eye on his mental health and to prove he never sneaked up to the surface. Witnesses monitored him day and night.

A Guinness adjudicator confirmed the record for the longest time living underwater without decompression, beating the previous mark of 100 days. He kept a copy of Jules Verne's Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea by his bed and says he admires Captain Nemo.

body.quote: He said the point was to show that the ocean could one day be a place for humans to live.

body: He celebrated his return to dry land with champagne, a cigar and a jump straight back into the Caribbean. He admitted he was a little sad the adventure was over. Whoever got to sit next to him afterwards, given the shower situation, was not asked for comment.

headline: Man Facing Car-Theft Charges Drives a Stolen Car to His Own Car-Theft Hearing
dek: An auto theft task force watched him park. He never made it in front of the judge.
body: There are bad ideas, and then there is driving a stolen car to court for your stolen-car case.

A 41-year-old man from Soledad, California, was due to appear at the Monterey County courthouse in Salinas on a pending auto theft charge. At around 11 a.m. on Tuesday, March 24, 2026, he pulled into the courthouse parking area, on time and ready to face the music.
The car he arrived in had been reported stolen in San Jose.

As luck would have it for everyone except him, members of a regional auto theft task force, known as MADCAT, were watching as he parked. Of all the parking lots in California, he had picked the one where car-theft specialists were literally on duty.

body.quote: Deputies met him right outside the courtroom where his car-theft case was about to be heard.

body: He was arrested before he could set foot in front of the judge. The sheriff's office said the arrest went smoothly.

He was booked into Monterey County Jail on suspicion of unlawfully taking a vehicle, committing a felony while out on bail, and driving on a suspended licence. His original case is presumably now the least of his problems.

headline: It's Official: A Judge Has Ruled That Tacos and Burritos Are Sandwiches
dek: A strip-mall rule said sandwiches only. A taco shop owner fought it for two years, and won.
body: The internet has argued for years about whether a hot dog is a sandwich. In Indiana, a court has settled a far bolder question.

The owner of a local restaurant called The Famous Taco wanted to open a second location in a Fort Wayne strip mall. There was one problem. The plaza was bound by an agreement with a neighbouring condo association that allowed only a sandwich-bar-style restaurant selling made-to-order, subway-style sandwiches. No alcohol. No outdoor seating. And, everyone assumed, no tacos.
The rule was reportedly designed to keep national fast-food chains out. When the local plan commission refused to amend it to explicitly allow tacos and burritos, the owner sued.

body.h2: The ruling heard round the lunch hour

body: After more than two years of legal back and forth, Allen Superior Court Judge Craig Bobay delivered his verdict in May 2024.

body.quote: Tacos and burritos, the judge wrote, are Mexican-style sandwiches.

body: Because the agreement never said the sandwiches had to be American-style, the judge concluded the taco shop had been allowed all along, and the whole fight to amend it had been unnecessary.
The owner said he was relieved and expected the new location to open within a few months. The hot dog question, sadly, remains open.

headline: Fugitive Otter 841 Keeps Stealing Surfboards and Outsmarting Wildlife Officials
dek: Nets, traps and a decoy surfboard all failed. Santa Cruz's most wanted sea otter just dived off and kept going.
body: Surfers off Santa Cruz spent the summer of 2023 dealing with an unusual hazard. Not sharks, not rip currents, but a five-year-old sea otter with a surfboard habit.

Known officially as Otter 841, the female southern sea otter developed a routine: swim up to a surfer, climb aboard, refuse to leave, and start biting the board. In one case she chewed off part of a board's nose.
Crime may run in the family. Otter 841 was born in captivity and released into the wild in June 2020, and her mother had also been captured for harassing kayakers.

Teams from the California Department of Fish and Wildlife and the Monterey Bay Aquarium spent weeks trying to catch her. They towed a baited surfboard toward their boat. They tried several kinds of nets. They deployed an underwater trap operated by divers.
Every time they got close, she simply dived off and swam away. Officials could not net her in open water, and sedating her was off the table because she could drown.

body.quote: A local photographer said the failed capture attempts had become almost comical.

body: Federal wildlife officials called her behaviour highly unusual and suggested hormones or people feeding her might be to blame. Meanwhile, she gained a fan club that gathered on the cliffs every day to watch. No humans were hurt, and as of late July she was still at large. Southern sea otters, once down to about 50 animals in 1938, now number around 3,000. At least one of them is very good at surfing.
